_note: Fictional sources for teaching: every source cited here is invented. See sources.json.
title: Who's speaking?
context: An engineering student is evaluating 3D-printed concrete for housing.
question: Mark each part of the paragraph: is it the source's idea, the writer's own, or both (the writer building on a source)?
text: [[s1:3D-printed concrete is often promoted as a fast, low-waste way to build affordable housing.]] [[s2:Its main structural weakness lies at the joins between printed layers, where the bond is weaker than within each layer {{cite:osei2020}}.]] [[s3:Laboratory tests have also found that this bond weakens further when walls cure at low temperatures {{cite:lindqvist2021}}.]] [[s4:Lindqvist's samples were small, however, and were cured in controlled conditions rather than on site.]] [[s5:Taken together, these findings suggest that printed housing may be less suited to cold climates than its promoters imply,]] [[s6:at least until methods that strengthen the joins between layers have been tested outside the laboratory.]]

s1.note: The writer's framing. It describes how the technology is promoted, as general background. (If this were a specific, contestable claim, it would need a citation.)

s2.note: Osei's finding, reported in the writer's words and cited.

s3.note: Lindqvist's finding. 'Also' is the writer's link, but the content is the source's.

s4.note: The facts about the samples come from the source, but 'however' turns them into the writer's evaluation of it.

s5.note: The writer's inference, built on both sources: 'Taken together' signals synthesis. No source says this on its own.

s6.note: The writer's own qualification, pointing to what is still unknown.

notes.text: In engineering, you'd almost never quote a source like this. You paraphrase the finding and cite it, as every sentence here does — so the writer's voice has to come through in how the findings are framed, linked and evaluated.
In numeric styles, a bare number tells the reader nothing about who is speaking. Naming the author when it matters — 'Lindqvist's samples were small' — makes it clear whose work is being evaluated.

chefsNote: If the reader can't tell the sauce from the dish, you've served soup.
